readerTitle: How to ask your boss for more people, money or time
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물류창고 야간 교대 리더, 소프트웨어 회사 엔지니어링 리더) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 자원 요청은 내 고충을 알리는 일이 아니라, 상사가 쉽게 결정할 수 있도록 요청과 비용과 대안을 정리해 건네는 일이다.
misconception: 얼마나 힘든지 충분히 설명하면 상사가 알아서 필요한 것을 줄 것이다.

sources.text: 모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 임시 피커 비용 계산: 2명 × 주 40시간 × 6주 × 시급 $18 = $8,640 (카드에는 약 $8,600으로 표기). 시급은 설명용 가정입니다.
소프트웨어 사례의 계약직 3개월 약 $30,000은 설명용 가정이며 지역·직무에 따라 크게 다릅니다. 카드에 '~'로 근사치임을 표시했습니다.
다음 레슨 예고(PPL-08-09, 2007년 아이폰 키노트)와 표현이 맞는지 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: "We're drowning. I need more people."
body: Dana runs the night shift at a regional warehouse. Peak season starts in five weeks, and her pickers are already working overtime.
She caught her boss, the operations director, in the hallway and said it plainly. Her boss listened for a minute, then said, "Everyone's stretched. Let's see how it goes."
Dana's problem was real. Her ask wasn't clear.

image.label: Warehouse supervisor talking to her boss in a busy aisle
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 밤 시간 물류창고 통로, 쌓인 상자와 지게차 사이에서 형광 조끼를 입은 교대 리더가 지나가던 상사에게 다급하게 말을 거는 장면. 상사는 휴대폰을 보며 걷는 중. 실제 기업 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Dana gets ten minutes on Thursday. How should she open?

options.text: "Let me tell you how hard the team's been pushing. Three people did double shifts last week."
options.feedback: It builds sympathy, but her boss still has to guess what decision is wanted. Effort stories describe the pain, not the ask.

options.text: "I'm asking for two temp pickers for the six weeks of peak, about $8,600. Without them, I expect late shipments like last year."
options.feedback: This is **clear communication**: bottom line first. In one breath her boss knows the decision, the price and the stakes.

options.text: "Did you get a chance to look at the spreadsheet I sent? It has all the order data."
options.feedback: The data may be solid, but it hands the thinking to a busy boss. Unopened attachments rarely win budget.

cards.eyebrow: The other side of the desk
cards.title: Her boss has a different problem.
body: The operations director has requests from four shift leads and one budget. She is judged on two things: on-time shipping and cost.
So Dana reframed her ask around those goals: "Two temps protect our on-time rate with our biggest client during the weeks it matters most."
This is **managing up**: understanding what your boss is measured on and what limits her, then making it easy for her to say yes.

image.label: A manager's desk with several competing requests
image.brief: 책상 위에 서로 다른 팀의 요청서 네 장이 놓여 있고, 그 옆에 "On-time %"와 "Budget"이라고 적힌 작은 계기판 두 개. 요청서 중 한 장만 계기판과 선으로 연결되어 강조됨. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.eyebrow: The shape of a good ask
cards.title: Dana's ten-minute version had four parts.

breakdown.label: The ask
breakdown.detail: Two temp pickers for six weeks, about $8,600

breakdown.label: Why now
breakdown.detail: Peak starts in five weeks, and agencies need time to find people

breakdown.label: Cost of no
breakdown.detail: Late shipments, more overtime, a worn-out crew

breakdown.label: A smaller option
breakdown.detail: One temp, or borrow two people from the day shift

cards.callout: Ask first. Reasons second. Options last.
cards.softwareNote: The same four parts work for a tool, a contractor or a delay to a deadline. Name the thing, the date, the cost of waiting and a cheaper fallback.

cards.title: Her boss says: "I can't add headcount. Budget's tight until next quarter."

options.text: Repeat the late-shipment numbers more firmly
options.feedback: Pressure without new information tells her you didn't hear her constraint. You may win this round and lose her trust for the next one.

options.text: "Understood. Is it the headcount line or total spend? Would one temp, or borrowing two from day shift, work?"
options.feedback: This is **managing up** in action. You learn her real limit and offer options she can actually approve.
It keeps the peace, but the risk goes silent. She can't plan for late shipments she doesn't know are coming.

cards.title: Your credibility is the real budget.
body: It's tempting to ask for four people to get two. Do it once and your boss learns to discount every number you bring.
Report back after a yes. If the temps kept shipments on time, say so with numbers. That makes the next ask easier.
And a no is often a "not now". Going over your boss's head without telling her usually costs more than the resource is worth.

cards.title: Now it's a software team.
body: Priya leads five engineers at a software company. Night-time alerts from the on-call rota are wearing two of them down, and a big release is due in April.
She wants a contractor for three months. Her CTO reads messages between meetings. Which message should she send?

options.text: "Hey, can we chat about on-call sometime? The team is really struggling."
options.feedback: Honest, but vague. With no clear decision or deadline, it's easy to push to next week. That's a **clear communication** gap.

options.text: "Asking for approval: one contractor for 3 months (~$30k) to take half of night on-call before the April release. If budget is tight, I could pause the reporting feature for a month instead. Need a decision by Friday."
options.feedback: Ask, cost, deadline and a fallback in four lines. It ties the request to the CTO's release goal, which is **managing up**.

options.text: A link to a six-page incident report with "Thoughts?"
options.feedback: The evidence helps, but there's no ask. Lead with the request and attach the report as backup.

cards.title: Make your ask easy to say yes to.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Clear communication:** lead with what you want, what it costs and by when. **Managing up:** frame it around your boss's goals and limits, and bring a smaller option.
**Try it today:** write your next request in three sentences. What you want, what happens if you don't get it, and one cheaper alternative.
